transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what brought you in to see me today?

Well, Doctor, I came because… at church, things have been getting strange with me. I’ll be helping, you know, by the potluck table, and then I’ll just stand there holding the serving spoon up in the air and not move. People are waiting, and I don’t know why I’m doing it.

And the napkins too—last Sunday, or maybe the one before, I kept folding the same little stack over and over. My hands just kept doing it. The ladies there, they’re nice, but I can tell they don’t know what to say. It makes me feel embarrassed.
Over these past couple of weeks, have you been feeling unusually sad, down, or losing interest in things you normally enjoy?

I don’t know that I’d call it sad, exactly. I mean, I still go to church and I like seeing the ladies there, when things are calm. Sometimes I get bothered because I feel foolish, but… sad? I’m not sure.

My interest, well, I still like the hymns. There’s one we used to sing when I was little—my mother liked that one, though I can’t always remember the words now. So no, I haven’t really noticed losing interest like that.
Have you been diagnosed with any medical or neurological conditions—like a thyroid problem, seizures, a head injury, or infection—especially anything new around the time these episodes started?

I’m not sure, Doctor. I don’t think anybody’s told me about those things… thyroid or seizures, I mean. I did go to the clinic once years ago, but that was more because my feet were bothering me, and the nurse had such pretty earrings, little blue stones—my aunt used to wear ones like that to Sunday service.

But new around when this started? I don’t really know of anything. Nobody said I had an infection or anything with my head. At least, not that I remember.
Have you ever heard voices or sounds that other people don't seem to hear, or had thoughts or beliefs that others told you weren't true?

I’m not sure how to answer that, Doctor. I don’t think I hear voices like you mean… not like someone standing there talking when nobody is there.

Sometimes I’ll think I heard something at church, like a chair moving or somebody whispering, but churches make all kinds of little sounds, you know. The old radiator used to clank in the church I went to as a girl, and everyone would look up during the sermon.

As for beliefs… people have told me I get mixed up sometimes, but I don’t know if that’s what you mean. I’m not trying to make things up.
Have you or your family noticed any recent changes in your memory, or times when you feel confused about where you are or what day it is?

I don’t really know, Doctor. I mean, I misplace things sometimes, but everyone does that, don’t they? My sister used to put her glasses right on top of her head and then fuss around the whole kitchen looking for them.

As for what day it is… I try to keep up with Sundays because of church. The bulletin helps, if they print it clear enough. I don’t think I’ve been getting lost or anything like that. I’m not sure my family would say different, though.
Can you tell me approximately how long ago these freezing and repetitive movement episodes first started, and whether they came on gradually over months or fairly suddenly over just a few days?

I think… maybe around six months, give or take. That’s when people started saying I was acting a little odd or not making sense when I talked. It’s hard for me to pin it down exactly, because the months sort of run together, especially after holidays—you know, you take down the decorations and then suddenly it’s Easter things in the stores.

I don’t know if it came all at once in a few days. It feels more like people just began noticing it over time, maybe over those months.
You mentioned people said you weren't making sense when you talked—can you tell me more about that? Do you find your thoughts jumping around or getting jumbled when you try to speak?

Yes… I think that’s what happens, sort of. I mean to answer plain when the ladies ask me something, like about the blankets we’re collecting or choir practice, and then my words just… run off.

I’ll start about the blankets, and then I’m talking about beans for supper, and then a hymn we used to sing, and then my roses out back. It all feels connected in my head at the time, but folks look at me like they can’t find where I’m going with it. Then I get embarrassed and try to stop.
During these episodes of freezing or repetitive movements, have you or anyone around you noticed things like your body becoming stiff or rigid, a fast heartbeat, sweating, or a fever?

Well… I don’t know about fever or heartbeat, I don’t really check those things. But it’s the odd stopping that’s been bothering folks.

At church, I’ll be by the potluck table and just stand there holding the serving spoon up, like I meant to put it down but didn’t. Or I’ll fold the same stack of napkins over and over while people are waiting, and then someone has to say my name. It’s embarrassing… the potluck ladies are kind, but you can tell they’re watching.
Around the time these episodes began about six months ago, were you started on any new medications, or did you begin using any new substances, alcohol, or over-the-counter drugs?

I’m not real sure. I don’t think there was some new pill right then, but I get my things mixed up sometimes… the bottles all look alike in the cabinet, and my daughter, she tells me to keep them lined up by the sink, but then I move them when I’m wiping the counter.

I don’t drink much, if that’s what you mean. And drugstore things… maybe aspirin or cold medicine here and there, but I can’t remember starting anything special when all that began.
In the months leading up to when these episodes started, did you notice any other physical changes, like losing weight without trying, feeling unusually tired, or having any illness or fever?

I’m not sure, doctor. I don’t keep track of my weight much… my daughter fusses with the scale more than I do.

Tired, well, I get tired, but I’m old, you know, and there’s always laundry or dishes or church things, and sometimes just getting ready takes half the morning. I don’t remember being sick with a fever before it started, not plain like that. If I was, I might’ve just thought it was a chill or something and made tea.
Compared to a year or so ago, would you say your ability to handle everyday tasks—like cooking, paying bills, or getting dressed—has noticeably declined, or has it stayed about the same?

I guess it’s… it’s slipped some, yes. Not so much the cooking or bills—well, I don’t want to say that wrong—but more with church things.

I used to help more with choir and little volunteer jobs, you know, making sure people had the right papers or where to stand, and now I mix up the plans, or I’ll think I told somebody and I didn’t. Then folks get uneasy, or someone has to redo what I was supposed to handle. So I’ve stepped back some. I don’t like it… church has always been where I felt useful.

Have you or your family noticed any new physical changes, like your hands shaking, your walk becoming stiff or shuffling, or your muscles feeling unusually tight, around the time these episodes began?

I don’t know that I noticed anything like that clear, no. My hands… well, they’re just old hands, they get clumsy with buttons sometimes, but I can’t say they were shaking new around then.

Walking, I still get where I’m going, though my daughter says I take too long in the grocery store—but that’s because people stop me and talk, and then I forget the list. Muscles tight… I’m not sure what you mean exactly. I didn’t think of it as something new starting with all this.

Has your family noticed whether your confusion and trouble finding the right words have been steadily getting worse over these six months, or do they seem to come and go rather than continuously worsen?

It’s more like… some days I can talk plain enough, and then other times it gets away from me. My daughter says I start in one place and end up somewhere else.

Like at church, if the ladies ask me about the blankets or choir practice, I mean to answer straight, I do, but then my words go off—beans, then hymns, then my roses out back—and they just look at me like they can’t find what I’m saying. I don’t always notice until their faces change.

No, I don’t think so… not when I was younger. I mean, I’ve always talked a lot, my sister used to say I could turn one story into three, especially after church suppers when everyone was cleaning up and I’d remember somebody’s casserole dish—

But this kind of thing, where folks say I’m not making sense or I get stuck there… that’s more recent. Maybe the last six months or so people have been noticing it. Before that, I don’t remember it being like this.
Has anyone in your close family—like a parent or sibling—ever been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease or another type of memory-related dementia?

I don’t rightly know. My mother… well, she got forgetful when she got old, but everybody said that’s just getting old, you know? She’d misplace her glasses and fuss about the mailman coming late, but I don’t remember any doctor giving it a name.

My brothers and sisters, I can’t say. We didn’t always talk about things like that. Folks kept their business close. So… no one I know of was told they had that, but I might not have been told either.
Have you or your family noticed times when you have trouble recognizing people you know well, or feel unsure about familiar places, like your own home or the church?

I don’t know that I’ve had that, not exactly. I know my people when I see them… I think I do. Sometimes I have to look a second, but then, you know, folks change their hair or they come in with a hat on, and at church everybody’s moving around and talking over coffee, and Miss Ellen always wears that blue coat except when she don’t—

My house still feels like my house. The church too. I don’t think I’ve been lost there. I might get turned around if someone moved the chairs after a luncheon, but that’s just… well, they’re always moving things.

Has your family noticed any changes in your personality or behavior—like saying or doing things that seem out of character, acting more withdrawn, or losing interest in things you used to care about—around the time these episodes started?

Well… my family says I’ve been acting strange, I suppose. That’s why I came, really. At church I keep doing odd things, and folks notice. Like I’ll be standing by the potluck table with the serving spoon held up in my hand and just… not moving. And somebody will say my name, and I’ll realize everybody’s waiting.

Or I’ll start folding napkins, the same little stack over and over, while people are trying to set the table. I don’t mean to hold things up. I used to help with all that just fine—potlucks need order, you know, because if the beans go next to the desserts then people make a mess of the whole line—but lately they look at me funny. My sister says it isn’t like me.

Has your family noticed you saying or doing things in front of others that seem embarrassing or out of place—like blurting out something rude, ignoring social manners, or not seeming to care how it looks to people around you?

Well… I don’t know if I’m being rude, exactly. I don’t mean to be. But yes, people at church look embarrassed for me sometimes. That’s part of why I came.

I’ll be by the potluck table, holding the serving spoon up like I’m about to dish something, and then I just… stand there. Not moving. And everyone’s waiting, you know, because the line backs up and the casseroles get cold. Or I’ll start folding the same little stack of napkins over and over, even when they need them set out. My sister says, “Come on now,” like I’m making a scene, but I’m not trying to. It just happens, and then I notice folks watching.

That’s what I was trying to say, Doctor. I came because at church I keep doing odd things, and people are noticing. Like I’ll be standing there by the potluck table with the serving spoon in my hand, just holding it up, and I don’t move. Everybody’s waiting on me, and I don’t even realize it right away.

Or I’ll be folding napkins, the same little stack over and over. I used to be good at helping with those things, you know, getting the tables right, making sure folks had what they needed… but now I get stuck on it somehow. It’s embarrassing when I look up and they’re all watching.

I’m not sure about that, Doctor. I mean… I still feel things, I think. If someone tells me something sad, I don’t like it. And happy news is nice.

My sister might say I don’t show it right, maybe, but she says a lot when she’s fussing with me. She always did like things done a certain way—at the church dinners she wants the plates stacked just so, and the green beans not too close to the pie because people drip sauce. I don’t know if that means I’m indifferent. I wouldn’t say I don’t care. I just… I’m not sure what they notice from the outside.

patient.answer:
Well, Doctor, I came because… at church, things have been getting strange with me. I’ll be helping, you know, by the potluck table, and then I’ll just stand there holding the serving spoon up in the air and not move. People are waiting, and I don’t know why I’m doing it.

And the napkins too—last Sunday, or maybe the one before, I kept folding the same little stack over and over. My hands just kept doing it. The ladies there, they’re nice, but I can tell they don’t know what to say. It makes me feel embarrassed.
